draft.title: Purpose, audience and context
card: Purpose
why the text was written. A writer may want to entertain, inform, persuade or reflect, and this shapes what goes in the text.
Audience
who the text is for. The audience affects the words, tone and examples a writer picks, such as slang for teenagers or technical terms for experts.
Context
when and where the text was made, and the values and events of that time and place. A text from 1950 may treat a topic differently from one made today.
To explain a writer's choice, ask three questions: why was this written, who is it for, and when and where was it made?
draft.remember: Ask why, who for, and when and where to explain a writer's choices.

a.q: A writer uses short, playful sentences and gaming slang in an article for 13-year-olds. Which idea best explains this choice?
opts: The audience is young, so the style suits them
The context is a different century from ours
The purpose is to give a formal legal warning
The writer wants to hide the topic from readers
a.why: The slang and playful tone are chosen to suit readers aged 13, so audience explains the choice. Context is about when and where a text was made, and nothing in the example points to a different century.
a.clue: Think about who the article is written for.

b.q: Priya writes a speech urging her school to ban single-use plastic bottles. She uses a firm tone and a list of reasons. Which choice is explained by her purpose?
opts: The firm tone and list of reasons to win support
The fact that she is writing in Australia today
The fact that her listeners are students and teachers
The use of a school hall as the place of delivery
b.why: Priya wants to persuade, so a firm tone and clear reasons serve that purpose. The other options describe audience or context: who is listening, and when and where the speech is given.
b.clue: Which choice helps her reach her goal, rather than describing who or where?

a.best: The audience is young, so the style suits them

b.best: The firm tone and list of reasons to win support

problems.detail: The wrong options ('formal legal warning', 'hide the topic', 'a different century') are plainly absurd for the example. The clue also says 'think about who the article is written for', which all but names the answer. This is too easy for Year 11 Advanced.

check.summary: The card, remember line and both answers are accurate. Question a is too easy, because its wrong options are implausible and its clue nearly gives the answer away.

a.q: In the same week, a scientist writes two texts, both published in Australia, explaining how a new vaccine works. One uses technical terms for a medical journal. The other uses simple comparisons for a children's magazine. What best explains the difference?
opts: Each text is written for a different audience
The texts come from different times and places
One text informs while the other persuades
The topic of the vaccine differs between texts
a.why: The topic, purpose, time and place are the same, so the readers explain the change: experts get technical terms and children get simple comparisons. Context cannot explain it, because both texts were published in Australia in the same week.
a.clue: Look at what stays the same across both texts, and what changes.

b.clue: Which choice helps her reach her goal, rather than describing who or where?
